rows.verified: Loud noise at work can damage hearing and create safety risks.
The Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 place legal duties on employers.
Employers should assess risks from workplace noise and identify workers who may be exposed.
Noise exposure should be eliminated or reduced so far as reasonably practicable.
Engineering and organisational controls should be considered before relying only on personal protection.
Suitable hearing protection should be provided and used where residual risk requires it.
Workers should receive information, instruction and training about noise hazards and controls.
Health surveillance should be arranged where noise exposure creates a risk to hearing.
Noise risk depends on sound level, frequency, duration, impulsiveness, distance, controls, hearing protection and individual susceptibility.
HSE noise evidence is task-, machine-, workplace-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level hearing-loss probability.
Lyme disease is a bacterial infection transmitted to humans through the bite of certain infected ticks.
Cases occur across the country, although reporting is more common in some regions including southern England.
An erythema migrans or bullseye-type rash commonly develops between 3 and 30 days after a tick bite.
A characteristic rash does not occur in every Lyme-disease case.
Recent tick exposure with compatible symptoms but no rash may require blood testing through NHS or UKHSA services.
Tick-bite avoidance, skin and clothing checks and prompt tick removal reduce exposure opportunities.
Ticks should be removed carefully without leaving mouthparts embedded or compressing the body.
UKHSA's Rare and Imported Pathogens Laboratory provides accredited confirmatory testing and specialist advice.
Lyme-disease risk depends on tick species, infection prevalence, attachment duration, habitat, behaviour, clothing, removal timing and host factors.
UKHSA Lyme evidence is tick-, exposure-, person-, laboratory-, geography- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
